newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tough spacewalks and repairs await new Mir crew.
newsitem.headline: Tough spacewalks and repairs await new Mir crew.

text.p: Cosmonauts Anatoly Solovyov and Pavel Vinogradov on Friday got a first-hand look at the crippled Mir space station they will have to repair in the coming weeks to save the craft.
The task before them is enormous, and if recent experience is a guide, other woes may develop even as they overcome some problems in the 11-year-old station.

The most pressing need ahead is to get one of two Elektron oxygen generating systems working. "The cosmonauts will come back to the search for the malfunction once the docking is fully over," Yuri Koptev, head of the Russian Space Agency, said after the new crew docked late on Thursday.

The newer Elektron in the Kvant-1 module has not worked since last week, and the older back up is in the Kvant-2 module, which has been switched off to save energy since Mir's June 25 accident, causing a major loss of power.
On Thursday, the crew installed a pressure regulator and another part from the back-up Elektron into the newer model, but the effort failed to revive the unit, NASA said.

The crew -- which consists of five cosmonauts until two Russians return to Earth next week -- are now seeking to run a new power line from the core module into Kvant-2 to power up the back-up Elektron separately, Russian officials said.

The two cosmonauts will undertake far riskier efforts on August 20, when they don bulky spacesuits inside Mir and enter a transition node at the end of the core module before sealing it off from the rest of the ship.

Solovyov, on his fifth mission to Mir, will then depressurise the cramped area and Vinogradov will open the hatch to the Spektr module, which suffered a puncture when it collided with the station's resupply craft on June 25.

Vinogradov will reach into and perhaps partly enter the dark, airless, 12-metre (yard) -long Spektr, the base for American astronauts on board Mir, to reconnect cables leading to its solar panels, three out of four of which are said to still work.

The two cosmonauts will also install a new hatch to allow the cables to carry power into the rest of Mir. But if it does not hold pressure, or if they cannot repressurise the transition node after resealing Spektr, they will have to abandon ship.
If chemicals or metal fragments that could be floating inside Spektr puncture Vinogradov's spacesuit, he would die instantly.
NASA astronaut Michael Foale will sit in the Soyuz escape capsule just a hatch away from the node during this repair.

The second phase of the Spektr repairs are scheduled to begin on September 3, when two cosmonauts leave Mir for a spacewalk to examine the puncture, an operation that carries different risks from the internal repair.

"At least in the internal spacewalk you don't have to worry about drifting away from the station," a NASA official said. "Basically you have the same overall problem of getting into a spacesuit and working in a vacuum."
"Outside you always have to be concerned about being properly tethered and things like that," he said. "There are projections outside of the Mir that also have to be avoided."

Russian officials have said they would like Foale to take part in the September 3 spacewalk with Solvoyov, a veteran of nine spacewalks in his previous four missions. NASA says the issue is under review.
Cosmonauts would repair the puncture at a later date.
